h: Make the most of the Causeway Coast
p: The Giant's Causeway became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986, and it's still the only one in Northern Ireland. Once you're down among the stones, look out for some of the formations with names that have stuck for generations: the Wishing Chair, a natural throne worn smooth by countless visitors, the Giant's Boot, and the Organ, a run of tall columns up the cliff that really does look like organ pipes.

A few tips for a good visit. The stones can be slippery, especially when wet or near the sea, so wear proper footwear and keep an eye on the kids. It can be wild and windy on this coast even in summer, so pack layers and a waterproof. And it's a steady walk back up from the shore, so if anyone in your group finds hills hard, ask about the shuttle bus that runs between the visitor centre and the stones.

Allow two to three hours for the visitor centre and the stones, or longer if you're tackling the clifftop paths. The Causeway is part of the Causeway Coast Way, so serious walkers can keep going for miles.

This stretch of coast is packed with things to combine with your visit. The village of Bushmills is home to the Old Bushmills Distillery, with its whiskey heritage going back centuries. Dunluce Castle, a dramatic ruin perched on the cliff edge, is a short drive west, and Carrick-a-Rede rope bridge is a short drive east if you fancy wobbling over a gap high above the sea. The Dark Hedges, the famous avenue of twisted beech trees, is also within easy reach.
